home.metaTitle: Affordable AI style & vibe match game
home.metaDescription: Upload one photo and get playful public-figure style matches built from written visible traits. Affordable, consent-first, no accounts, no face recognition — and your photo is never stored.
home.whatIsBody1: Twinzy is a low-cost browser game that looks at one photo you choose, writes down the visible style traits it can see — hair color and length, glasses, beard style, face shape, overall look — and then suggests public figures whose publicly known style has a similar overall vibe. It is a playful style-twin generator, not a lookalike finder and not an identification tool.
home.whatIsBody2: The whole experience is a single round: you pick a photo, confirm you are happy for it to be analyzed, and within moments you get a short, readable list of playful matches with a score, a reason, and the exact traits that drove each suggestion. There is no account, no profile, and nothing to install.
home.howBody1: When you press analyze, our server reads your photo once and turns what is visible into a short written description — then the photo is wiped from memory immediately, whether the round succeeds or fails. From that moment on, only the written description exists anywhere in the game.
home.howBody2: Those written traits are compared against publicly known style descriptions of public figures, scored for overall vibe similarity, and returned as ranked playful matches. The how-it-works page walks through every step in order, including exactly what the AI is allowed to do at each stage.
home.privacyValueBody1: Most photo apps store your image; Twinzy is built so it cannot. Your photo is processed only in memory, is never written to disk, never logged, and never used to train anything. Once its visible traits have been written down, the image is gone for good.
home.privacyValueBody2: There is no face recognition and no biometric template of any kind: matching happens purely over written text like "short curly hair" or "round glasses". The privacy page explains exactly what is processed in a round and what never leaves it.
home.limitsTitle: What the AI can and cannot do
home.limitsBody1: The AI only describes what is visible in a single photo, so lighting, angle, filters, and image quality directly change the result. Two photos of the same person can produce different matches — that is expected, because it reads style, not identity.
home.limitsBody2: It cannot recognize who you are, cannot judge beauty, personality, or character, and refuses to guess anything sensitive. When a photo is too unclear for a confident playful answer, it says so honestly instead of inventing one.
home.safetyBody1: Every AI answer is checked against strict rules before you see it: no identifying real people, no guesses about ethnicity, religion, health, or other sensitive traits, and no clinical or biometric language. Anything that breaks a rule is rejected or cleaned before display.
home.safetyBody2: These are not settings that can be switched off — they are enforced in code on every single round. The AI-safety page describes each principle and why it exists.
home.resultsBody1: Each match shows a rank, a style-similarity score, and a plain-language reason listing which written traits matched well, which were weak, and where there were clear mismatches. The score describes overall vibe overlap — never how much you "look like" someone.
home.resultsBody2: Treat every result as a playful conversation starter. It can be wrong, it changes with photo quality, and it never means you resemble, are related to, or share anything with the matched person beyond a written style description.
home.guidesTeaserIntro: Short, practical guides on the photo factors that most change your written traits and score — none of them require playing the game to be useful.

about.metaDescription: Twinzy is a privacy-first entertainment project: one photo becomes a short written style description, the photo is wiped, and playful text-only matches are suggested. Learn who built it and why.
about.title: About Twinzy
about.intro: Twinzy is a small, privacy-first entertainment project with one job: turn a single photo into a playful, text-based style match — and forget the photo immediately.
about.storyBody1: Twinzy started with a simple observation: people love "who is your style twin" games, but almost every one of them quietly collects faces. We wanted the fun without the collection — a game that could be enjoyed for a minute and then leave no trace at all.
about.storyBody2: So the pipeline was designed backwards from a single promise: the photo may be read once, in memory, and never kept. Everything else — the text-only matching, the wipe-in-every-case handling, the refusal to identify anyone — follows from that starting point.
about.differentBody1: Twinzy never compares faces. The moment your photo is analyzed it becomes a short written description — "wavy shoulder-length hair, thin-frame glasses, warm smile" — and only that text travels through the rest of the game. The image itself is already gone.
about.differentBody2: That design makes the fun part fully explainable: you can see exactly which written traits drove each suggestion, because written traits are all the system ever has to work with.
about.neverBody1: It will never tell you who you are, claim you look identical to a real person, or guess anything sensitive — ethnicity, religion, health, personality, attractiveness, and income are permanently out of bounds, and those limits are enforced in code, not just in policy.
about.neverBody2: It will also never store, share, or train on your photo. There are no accounts and no galleries; every round starts clean and ends clean.
about.moneyBody1: The game costs only a small, clearly shown fee per analysis — you always see the exact price before you pay. To keep it running we may also show a small number of clearly separated ads on content pages like this one — never inside the game and never next to your results — and we accept entirely optional support payments.
about.moneyBody2: If a paid option is ever offered, its exact price is shown clearly before you pay, and paying never changes what happens to your photo: nothing is ever stored either way.
about.technologyBody1: Twinzy runs on a small web stack with a vision-capable AI model (Google's Gemini API) used for exactly one step: reading the visible traits of your photo into text. Matching, scoring, and explanation all happen over that text afterwards.
about.technologyBody2: Every AI response is validated against a strict schema and a safety filter before it reaches your screen, so a malformed or unsafe answer is dropped rather than shown.
about.contactBody1: The FAQ answers the most common questions about privacy, accuracy, and how rounds work, and the help page covers quick troubleshooting for failed rounds and unclear photos.
about.contactBody2: Spotted something wrong, unclear, or unsafe? We genuinely want to know — the project improves fastest when players tell us exactly what confused or concerned them.

howItWorks.metaDescription: Every step of a Twinzy round, in order: explicit consent, one in-memory read of your photo into written traits, immediate deletion, text-only matching, and scored, explained results.
howItWorks.title: How Twinzy works
howItWorks.intro: A complete round takes under a minute. Here is every step in order, including what happens to your photo and what the AI is allowed to do at each stage.
howItWorks.consentBody1: You pick a photo from your device or take one with your camera, and you tick an explicit consent box that describes exactly what will happen: visible traits will be read from the photo, and everything afterwards works on text only.
howItWorks.consentBody2: Nothing is uploaded until you press analyze. Closing the tab or cancelling at any point aborts the round and clears the photo.
howItWorks.extractionBody1: Our server sends the photo to the AI exactly once and asks a narrow question: what is visibly there? The answer comes back as short written traits — hair color and texture, glasses, facial hair, face shape, expression, apparent style — plus notes about anything unclear.
howItWorks.extractionBody2: The AI is instructed not to guess who you are and not to infer anything sensitive; it describes only what a stranger could see at a glance.
howItWorks.wipeBody1: Immediately after the traits are extracted, the photo is deleted from server memory — on success, on failure, and on cancellation alike. It is never written to disk, never logged, and never cached.
howItWorks.wipeBody2: From this point the game holds only a text description. Nothing remains that could identify your face.
howItWorks.matchingBody1: The written traits are compared with publicly known style descriptions of public figures. Because this stage only ever receives text, it is structurally impossible for it to compare your face with anyone's face.
howItWorks.matchingBody2: Candidates are suggested for overall style and vibe similarity — hair, glasses, expression, general aesthetic — not for facial geometry.
howItWorks.scoringBody1: Each candidate is scored for how much of the written description overlaps, then the top matches come back with a rank, a percentage-style score, and a readable reason: which traits matched strongly, which were weak, and which clearly conflicted.
howItWorks.scoringBody2: If you play in Arabic, the finished result is translated as text so the explanation stays natural in your language — the photo plays no part in translation.
howItWorks.seeNeverTitle: What the AI sees — and never sees
howItWorks.seeNeverBody1: Sees once: the single photo you chose, in memory. Sees always: written visible traits. Never sees: your name, your location, your contacts, any other photos, or any identity information.
howItWorks.seeNeverBody2: Never produces: identifications, exact-lookalike claims, or sensitive judgments. Those are blocked by validation that runs on every AI answer, every round.
howItWorks.confidenceAndLimitsTitle: Confidence, uncertainty, and why results vary
howItWorks.confidenceAndLimitsBody1: Every extracted trait carries a confidence level, and any trait the AI could not read clearly — hidden by shadow, angle, hair, or a low-resolution crop — is marked unclear rather than guessed. Your result page lists both: matched traits and the ones the model was unsure about, so a low-confidence match is visible, never hidden.
howItWorks.confidenceAndLimitsBody2: Two photos of the same person, or even two attempts with the same photo, can land on different matches when several traits sit close to a borderline description — that is expected variation in a written-language judgment, not a bug. Our guides page has practical, photo-by-photo advice for tightening that variation.

guides.indexMetaTitle: Guides — get a clearer, more confident result
guides.indexMetaDescription: Practical, specific guides on the photo factors — lighting, angle, framing, styling — that change what Twinzy's AI can read from a photo, plus how to understand your score.
guides.indexIntro: Twinzy reads a single photo and turns what is visible into a short written description; everything downstream depends on how clearly that description could be written. These guides explain the photo factors that matter most, and how to read what comes back — useful whether or not you ever open the game.

bestPhoto.metaTitle: How to Choose the Best Photo for Accurate AI Style Results
bestPhoto.metaDescription: What actually makes a photo work well for AI trait analysis: framing, recency, filters, and the mistakes that most often produce a weak or uncertain result.
bestPhoto.navTeaser: What actually makes a photo easy for the AI to read clearly.
bestPhoto.title: How to choose the best photo for accurate AI style results
bestPhoto.intro: Twinzy's AI only ever works from one photo, read once. A photo that shows your face clearly, honestly, and mostly unobstructed gives it far more to work with than one that does not — here is what that means in practice.
bestPhoto.section1Title: What the AI is actually reading
bestPhoto.section1Body1: The model looks for visible, describable traits: hair color and texture, glasses, facial hair, face shape, expression, apparent style. It is not measuring geometry or checking an identity — it is writing down what a stranger glancing at the photo would notice.
bestPhoto.section1Body2: That means anything that hides those details — not just your face itself, but hair covering your forehead, glasses reflecting light, or a hand near your jaw — removes information the AI never gets a chance to describe.
bestPhoto.section2Body1: A head-and-shoulders crop where your face fills a reasonable portion of the frame works best. Too far away and detail is lost to low resolution; too close and features get cropped out of frame entirely.
bestPhoto.section2Body2: One person, one face. A group photo, a photo with someone partially in frame, or a heavily cropped selfie all make it harder for the extraction step to know which face — or which details — it should be describing.
bestPhoto.section3Body1: A current photo, taken in roughly the last year, reflects how you actually look now — a hairstyle, beard, or glasses that have since changed will simply produce a description of the old photo, not you.
bestPhoto.section3Body2: Heavy beauty filters, smoothing, or face-reshaping edits change the very traits the AI is trying to read. An unfiltered photo, even an imperfect one, is more useful than a heavily edited one.
bestPhoto.section4Body1: Sunglasses or a face mask hide entire trait categories — eyes and eyebrows, or the mouth and jaw — leaving the model with nothing to describe there. Extreme close-crop selfies that cut off the top of the head or chin do something similar.
bestPhoto.section4Body2: None of these mistakes break the game; the extraction step still runs. They simply produce a result with more traits marked uncertain, since an honest "unclear" is what the system returns instead of guessing.
bestPhoto.tip1: Keep your face fully unobstructed — no sunglasses, mask, or hand near the jaw or forehead
bestPhoto.tip2: Use a photo from roughly the last year, matching your current hair and facial hair
bestPhoto.tip3: Skip heavy filters, smoothing, or face-reshaping edits
bestPhoto.tip4: Face mostly toward the camera, with head and shoulders inside the frame

lighting.metaTitle: Why Lighting Changes AI Photo Analysis
lighting.metaDescription: How lighting direction, backlighting, and color casts change which visible traits an AI model can confidently read from a photo — and how to set up better light.
lighting.navTeaser: How shadows and backlighting quietly hide the details the AI needs.
lighting.title: Why lighting changes AI photo analysis
lighting.intro: Lighting decides how much of your face is actually visible in the pixels the AI receives — not just how flattering the photo looks. Poor lighting is one of the single biggest causes of a low-confidence result.
lighting.section1Body1: Hard, single-direction light casts shadows that can hide half a face's detail — a jawline lost in shadow, an eyebrow shape flattened by harsh overhead light. The AI can only describe what the image actually shows, so a shadowed region often comes back marked uncertain rather than described.
lighting.section1Body2: This is not the AI being cautious for no reason: it is reporting genuine ambiguity in the source image, the same way a person squinting at a dark photo would struggle to describe a shadowed feature confidently.
lighting.section2Body1: A bright window or the sun directly behind you turns your face into a silhouette to the camera, even if it looks fine to your own eyes in the moment. The photo file itself often has far less facial detail than the scene appeared to have.
lighting.section2Body2: This is the single most common cause of a heavily uncertain result — more than any other lighting mistake — because it can obscure nearly every trait at once rather than just one region.
lighting.section3Body1: Strongly colored light — warm indoor bulbs, colored signage, a sunset — can shift how hair color or skin tone reads in the photo file, even though your eyes automatically correct for it in person.
lighting.section3Body2: Neutral, white-balanced light (daylight or a normal white light bulb) keeps colors closer to how they actually look, which keeps the written description closer to accurate too.
lighting.section4Body1: Face a window during the day, or face any even light source in a room — the goal is light falling on your face, not behind it. Overcast daylight is one of the most reliable, flattering, and evenly diffused light sources available.
lighting.section4Body2: Avoid a single hard light source to one side if you can — a second, softer fill light (or simply facing a bright wall) reduces the harsh shadow that hides half a face's traits.
lighting.tip1: Face a light source — window or lamp — rather than having it behind you
lighting.tip2: Overcast daylight or soft indoor light beats harsh direct sun or a single hard bulb
lighting.tip3: Avoid strong backlighting from a window or the sun behind you
lighting.tip4: Avoid deep shadow across one whole side of the face

cameraAngles.metaTitle: How Camera Angles Affect Face and Style Analysis
cameraAngles.metaDescription: Why a straight-on, eye-level photo reads more clearly than an extreme angle, and what camera distance and tilt do to AI trait analysis.
cameraAngles.navTeaser: Why a straight-on, eye-level shot outperforms an artistic angle.
cameraAngles.title: How camera angles affect face and style analysis
cameraAngles.intro: A flattering angle for a photo and a clear angle for AI analysis are not always the same thing. Here is what actually changes when the camera moves.
cameraAngles.section1Body1: A face turned mostly toward the camera gives the extraction step the most complete view: both eyes, both eyebrows, the full jawline, the whole hairstyle. A steep three-quarter or profile turn hides one entire side of the face from the camera by definition, not by any fault of the photo quality.
cameraAngles.section1Body2: The traits on the hidden side are not invented — they come back genuinely marked as not visible, which is the honest outcome, but it does mean less of the description has anything to work with.
cameraAngles.section2Body1: A camera held well above or below eye level foreshortens the face — a low upward angle can visually shorten the forehead, a high downward angle can visually shorten the chin. These are optical effects of the angle, not changes to how you look.
cameraAngles.section2Body2: An eye-level camera avoids this distortion entirely and is the closest thing to a neutral, representative view of your face.
cameraAngles.section3Body1: Too far back and the face becomes a small, low-detail region of a larger image — fine detail like eyebrow shape or lip outline can fall below what the model can confidently describe. Too close and the edges of the face (hairline, ears, chin) can crop out of frame.
cameraAngles.section3Body2: A distance where your head and shoulders comfortably fill the frame, without cropping the top of the head or the chin, is the reliable middle ground.
cameraAngles.section4Title: What an unclear angle looks like in your result
cameraAngles.section4Body1: Your result's image-quality section reports a face-angle and camera-distance impression alongside a general confidence level — if a photo was taken from a steep angle or a long distance, that shows up there directly rather than silently lowering the score with no explanation.
cameraAngles.section4Body2: If you see camera angle or distance called out as a limitation on a result, that is a specific, fixable thing about the photo, not a comment on you.
cameraAngles.tip1: Hold the camera at roughly eye level, not sharply above or below
cameraAngles.tip2: Face mostly toward the camera rather than in profile
cameraAngles.tip3: Keep your whole head and shoulders inside the frame
cameraAngles.tip4: Stand close enough that facial features are clearly resolved, not a small part of the frame

similarityScores.metaDescription: What Twinzy's style/vibe percentage actually measures, how matching, weak, and mismatched traits work, and why confidence and results can vary between attempts.
similarityScores.navTeaser: What the percentage measures, and how to read matching versus weak traits.
similarityScores.title: Understanding Twinzy similarity scores
similarityScores.intro: Every match comes back with a percentage, a rank, and a written reason. Here is what each of those actually represents — and what they deliberately do not claim.
similarityScores.section1Body1: The score is an estimate of overlap between your written visible traits and the public figure's publicly known style description — hair, glasses, expression, general aesthetic. It is a style/vibe fit estimate, not a facial-similarity measurement, and it is never calculated from face geometry because no face geometry is ever measured.
similarityScores.section1Body2: A high score means many written traits lined up; it does not mean, and is never presented as meaning, that you resemble that person's actual face.
similarityScores.section2Body1: Every result breaks its reasoning into matching traits (clear overlap), weak traits (a soft, lower-confidence signal), and watch-outs (traits that visibly differ from the suggested match). All three are shown together, not just the flattering ones.
similarityScores.section2Body2: Reading these three groups tells you far more than the percentage alone — a high score with several watch-outs and a low score with none can both be informative in their own way.
similarityScores.section3Body1: Separate from the match score, each extracted trait carries its own confidence level, and any image limitation — poor lighting, an unclear angle, low resolution — is listed explicitly rather than folded silently into the score.
similarityScores.section3Body2: A result built from a handful of low-confidence traits deserves less weight than one built from several high-confidence ones, even at the same percentage — the confidence detail is there to make that visible.
similarityScores.section4Body1: Traits that sit close to the boundary between two written descriptions — a hairstyle that could reasonably be called either "wavy" or "loosely curled", for instance — can tip either way between attempts. That is a property of describing something in language, not a malfunction.
similarityScores.section4Body2: A clearer photo narrows that boundary. Our guide on choosing a photo and our checklist for weak results both address the specific factors that most reduce this kind of variation.
similarityScores.tip1: Read the written reason, not only the percentage
similarityScores.tip2: Check the weak traits and watch-outs — they are shown deliberately, not hidden
similarityScores.tip3: A lower score usually traces back to photo clarity, not a judgment about you
similarityScores.tip4: An unclear photo widens uncertainty across every trait, not just one

aiVsFaceRecognition.metaTitle: AI Similarity Matching vs Face Recognition: What's the Difference
aiVsFaceRecognition.metaDescription: How biometric face recognition actually works, how Twinzy's text-only style matching is architecturally different, and what that difference means for privacy and accuracy.
aiVsFaceRecognition.navTeaser: Why text-only style matching is a different technology from biometric recognition.
aiVsFaceRecognition.title: AI similarity matching vs face recognition: what's the difference
aiVsFaceRecognition.intro: "AI and a photo" covers a lot of very different technology. Twinzy is deliberately not the kind most people picture when they hear "facial recognition" — here is the actual distinction.
aiVsFaceRecognition.section1Body1: Face recognition systems measure a face's geometry — the distances and proportions between features — and convert that into a numeric template (an embedding) that can be directly compared against other faces, often to answer "is this the same person".
aiVsFaceRecognition.section1Body2: That template is derived from the image itself and typically persists so it can be compared again later, which is exactly the kind of biometric data protection law treats with particular care.
aiVsFaceRecognition.section2Body1: The photo is read once for its visible, describable traits — hair, glasses, face shape, expression, apparent style — which are written down as short text. No facial geometry is measured, and no numeric face template is ever created, stored, or compared.
aiVsFaceRecognition.section2Body2: From that point forward, matching runs purely over text: comparing a written description against other written descriptions. It is structurally incapable of comparing your face to anyone else's face, because no face data exists past that first step.
aiVsFaceRecognition.section3Title: Why the distinction matters for privacy
aiVsFaceRecognition.section3Body1: Because no biometric template is ever created, there is nothing that could later be leaked, reused, matched against another database, or subject to the same regulatory scrutiny as stored biometric data — the risk category simply does not apply here.
aiVsFaceRecognition.section3Body2: The photo itself is deleted from memory immediately after its traits are written down, so even the source image is gone well before matching starts.
aiVsFaceRecognition.section4Title: What this means for accuracy expectations
aiVsFaceRecognition.section4Body1: A style/vibe match is an impression built from a handful of visible, describable traits — not an identity claim verified against measured geometry. It is designed to be a fun, honest estimate, and it is built to say so plainly rather than imply more precision than it has.
aiVsFaceRecognition.section4Body2: If you are looking for identity verification, age estimation, or any biometric security use, that is a genuinely different technology and Twinzy is not built for it — by design, not by limitation.
aiVsFaceRecognition.tip1: No face template or embedding is ever created
aiVsFaceRecognition.tip2: The photo is deleted before any matching happens, not after
aiVsFaceRecognition.tip3: Results are style impressions, phrased as such — never identity claims
aiVsFaceRecognition.tip4: There is nothing biometric stored to compare against later, because nothing is stored

hairstylesFaceShape.metaTitle: How Hairstyles Change Perceived Face Shape
hairstylesFaceShape.metaDescription: Why hair is one of the strongest visible-style signals an AI reads from a photo, and how hairline visibility and hairstyle changes shift your Twinzy result.
hairstylesFaceShape.navTeaser: How hair volume and hairline visibility shift the visible framing of a face.
hairstylesFaceShape.title: How hairstyles change perceived face shape
hairstylesFaceShape.intro: Hair is one of the most visually dominant traits in any photo, and it is read as one. A haircut between two photos of the same person is one of the most common reasons for a genuinely different-feeling result — and that is expected.
hairstylesFaceShape.section1Title: Why hair is such a strong signal
hairstylesFaceShape.section1Body1: Hair frames the whole face: its volume, length, and shape at the temples and jaw all change the silhouette a viewer — human or AI — perceives before looking at any individual feature. It is one of the first things described in every extraction.
hairstylesFaceShape.section1Body2: That is exactly why a public figure's known hairstyle carries real weight in a style match: it is often the single most visually recognizable style element they have.
hairstylesFaceShape.section2Title: How volume and framing read visually
hairstylesFaceShape.section2Body1: Fuller hair at the sides tends to visually soften a face's outline; hair pulled back or cropped short exposes more of the jaw and temple line underneath. Neither changes anything about the face itself — only what a photo shows.
hairstylesFaceShape.section2Body2: This is a description of visual framing in a single photo, never a measurement of head or skull shape — the AI is reporting an impression, the same way a stylist would when suggesting a cut.
hairstylesFaceShape.section3Body1: Hair, a hat, or a hood covering the forehead removes that whole region from what the AI can describe — hairline shape and forehead proportions come back marked unclear rather than guessed.
hairstylesFaceShape.section3Body2: If you want the fullest possible trait read, a photo with the hairline visible gives the extraction step more to work with, though it is entirely optional — an unclear hairline just means one fewer confidently-described trait.
hairstylesFaceShape.section4Title: What this means for your result
hairstylesFaceShape.section4Body1: A recent haircut, a grown-out style, or simply hair worn differently on a given day can shift which traits are described and, in turn, which public figures come back as matches.
hairstylesFaceShape.section4Body2: That is not the game being inconsistent — it is accurately describing a photo that is genuinely different from the last one, the same way any honest description would change.
hairstylesFaceShape.tip1: A photo with the hairline at least partly visible gives a fuller trait read
hairstylesFaceShape.tip2: Use a recent photo that reflects your current haircut
hairstylesFaceShape.tip3: Hats and hoods hide hairline detail — fine to wear, just expect that trait marked unclear
hairstylesFaceShape.tip4: A different hairstyle between two photos naturally changes the description, and that's expected

glassesFaceShape.metaDescription: How glasses are read as a visible style trait, why reflections and tinted lenses reduce confidence around the eyes, and what changes when you add or remove them.
glassesFaceShape.navTeaser: Why lens reflections and frame style change what's visible around your eyes.
glassesFaceShape.title: Glasses and face-shape styling guide
glassesFaceShape.intro: Glasses sit directly over one of the most detailed regions of the face, so they have an outsized effect on both what the AI can see and how a style match reads.
glassesFaceShape.section1Title: Why glasses are such a strong visible trait
glassesFaceShape.section1Body1: Frame shape, thickness, and color are explicitly described as part of every extraction, alongside the eyes and eyebrows underneath. Glasses (or their absence) are one of the more visually distinctive, easily-compared style choices a public figure can have.
glassesFaceShape.section1Body2: That makes them genuinely useful signal for a style match — but only when the eye region itself is still clearly visible through them.
glassesFaceShape.section2Body1: Glare across a lens, or lenses tinted enough to obscure the eyes, hides exactly the detail — eye shape, eyebrow line — that sits right behind them. That comes back as reduced confidence in that specific region, not a wrong guess.
glassesFaceShape.section2Body2: This is one of the more fixable causes of a partially uncertain result: a small change in angle relative to the light source is often enough to remove the glare.
glassesFaceShape.section3Body1: Thin, minimal frames read as a different visible style signal than bold, thick, or brightly colored ones — the same way they would to a stylist. This is read as-is from the photo; no assumption is made about the frames beyond what is visible.
glassesFaceShape.section3Body2: Sunglasses are a special case: they do not just tint the eye region, they typically hide it entirely, so that whole trait category returns as not visible rather than estimated.
glassesFaceShape.section4Title: What this means for your matches
glassesFaceShape.section4Body1: Adding or removing glasses between two photos of yourself changes a real, visible part of the description — expect that to shift which style matches come back, the same way a genuine haircut change would.
glassesFaceShape.section4Body2: Neither photo is more "correct" than the other; each is an honest description of what that specific photo showed.
glassesFaceShape.tip1: Clean lenses and a slight angle away from direct light reduce glare
glassesFaceShape.tip2: Avoid photos with strong reflections across the lenses if you can retake the shot
glassesFaceShape.tip3: Sunglasses hide the eye region entirely — fine to wear, but expect that trait marked not visible
glassesFaceShape.tip4: Frame color and shape are read as they appear, with no assumption beyond what's visible

weakResultsChecklist.metaTitle: Common Reasons AI Photo Analysis Produces Weak Results
weakResultsChecklist.metaDescription: A practical troubleshooting checklist for a low-confidence or fallback Twinzy result: lighting, angle, filters, occlusion, and framing, with a fix for each.
weakResultsChecklist.navTeaser: A quick troubleshooting checklist if your result came back uncertain.
weakResultsChecklist.title: Common reasons AI photo analysis produces weak results
weakResultsChecklist.intro: If your result came back with a lot of uncertain traits, or no confident match at all, it is almost always one of a small number of fixable photo issues — not a limitation you can't do anything about. Here is the checklist, in order of how often each one is the actual cause.
weakResultsChecklist.section1Body1: The single most common cause. Dim rooms, backlighting from a window, or a single hard light source casting deep shadow across half the face all hide detail the AI needs, and it reports that honestly as reduced confidence rather than inventing detail that was never visible.
weakResultsChecklist.section1Body2: Fix: retake the photo in even daylight, or face a light source rather than having it behind you. Our lighting guide covers this in more depth.
weakResultsChecklist.section2Body1: A steep profile angle, a photo taken from far away, or anything covering the face — a hand, a mask, hair across the eyes — reduces how much of the face the extraction step actually has to describe.
weakResultsChecklist.section2Body2: Fix: retake at eye level, facing mostly toward the camera, close enough that features are clearly resolved, with the face unobstructed.
weakResultsChecklist.section3Title: Heavy filters or very low resolution
weakResultsChecklist.section3Body1: Beauty filters, smoothing, or face-reshaping edits change the actual visible traits in the file, and a heavily compressed or low-resolution image simply does not contain enough detail to describe confidently.
weakResultsChecklist.section3Body2: Fix: use the original, unedited photo at its full resolution rather than a filtered or heavily compressed copy.
weakResultsChecklist.section4Title: Multiple people or the wrong subject in frame
weakResultsChecklist.section4Body1: A group photo, or a photo where someone else is more prominent in frame than you are, can make it unclear which face the description should be based on.
weakResultsChecklist.section4Body2: Fix: use a photo where you are the clear, single subject, ideally cropped to head and shoulders.
weakResultsChecklist.tip1: Retake in even daylight, facing a light source rather than having it behind you
weakResultsChecklist.tip2: Face the camera at eye level with your whole face unobstructed
weakResultsChecklist.tip3: Use the original, unfiltered photo at full resolution
weakResultsChecklist.tip4: Make sure you're the single, clear subject of the photo

aiSafety.metaDescription: The safety rules Twinzy enforces in code on every round: no identification, no sensitive inference, consent before processing, validated and filtered AI output, and honest limitations.
aiSafety.title: AI safety at Twinzy
aiSafety.intro: A game that points an AI at a personal photo has to be strict about what that AI may and may not do. These are the rules Twinzy enforces on every round — in code, not just in policy.
aiSafety.noIdentityBody1: Twinzy never determines or guesses who is in a photo. Matches are framed as playful style similarity to public figures, and wording that asserts identity — "this is", "you are", "exact lookalike" — is rejected before anything is displayed.
aiSafety.noIdentityBody2: This is also why Twinzy cannot become a face search: the matching stage never receives the photo at all, only written traits, so there is no face to search with.
aiSafety.noSensitiveBody1: The AI is forbidden from inferring ethnicity, religion, health, sexuality, personality, attractiveness, or income. Plain visible descriptors such as skin tone or hair texture may be described; conclusions about who or what a person is may not.
aiSafety.noSensitiveBody2: Any answer that crosses that line is discarded, and the round either retries safely or fails openly — unsafe content is never quietly shown.
aiSafety.consentFirstBody1: The photo is processed only after you tick a consent box whose wording describes the actual pipeline — visible-trait extraction followed by text-only matching. If the copy and the code ever disagreed, we would treat that as a bug of the highest severity.
aiSafety.consentFirstBody2: Consent applies to a single round. There is no standing permission, because nothing is retained between rounds.
aiSafety.validationTitle: Every answer is checked before you see it
aiSafety.validationBody1: AI output is machine-validated against a strict schema — structure, fields, score ranges — and a safety filter that rejects forbidden wording, sensitive topics, and clinical biometric phrasing, before it is shown or shared.
aiSafety.validationBody2: A response that fails either check is dropped. This runs at every stage — trait extraction, matching, translation — not just on the final answer.
aiSafety.limitationsBody1: The model reads one photo, once, and photos vary — so results vary. Lighting, angle, resolution, and filters all shift the written traits and therefore the matches. A different photo of you is genuinely a different round.
aiSafety.limitationsBody2: Public-figure style descriptions are also imperfect and change over time. Scores are best read as "how much of the written description overlapped", not as any deeper truth about you.
aiSafety.feedbackBody1: If a result ever seems to identify someone, make a sensitive claim, or otherwise break these rules, treat it as a bug — that is exactly what the validation layer exists to prevent.
aiSafety.feedbackBody2: Stop using that result and tell us through the routes described on the about page; safety reports get priority over everything else.

faq.metaDescription: Answers to the most common questions about Twinzy: face recognition, photo storage, accuracy, cost, accounts, the AI used, sharing, failed rounds, and child safety.
faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.intro: Short, honest answers to the questions players ask most.
faq.a1: No. Face recognition compares biometric measurements of faces. Twinzy converts your photo into written style traits, deletes the photo, and matches only over that text. No face templates or embeddings are ever created.
faq.a2: No. It is processed in server memory for the seconds needed to read visible traits, then wiped — on success, failure, and cancellation alike. It is never saved, logged, cached, or used for training.
faq.q3: Will Twinzy tell me who I look like exactly?
faq.a3: No. It suggests public figures with a similar overall style and vibe based on written traits, with a score and reasons. It never claims identity or an exact resemblance — that is a deliberate safety rule, not a missing feature.
faq.q4: Why do I get different results from different photos?
faq.a4: Because the AI can only describe what it sees in that specific photo. Lighting, angle, expression, and image quality change the written traits, and the traits are all the matcher ever receives.
faq.a5: Just a small fee per analysis — the exact price is always shown clearly before you pay, and you are only charged when the analysis actually runs. We may also show a small number of ads on content pages — never in the game or next to results — and accept optional support.
faq.a6: No. There are no accounts, profiles, or sign-ins. Every round is independent and leaves nothing behind.
faq.a7: The server uses Google's Gemini API for one narrow task: describing the visible traits of your photo as text. Matching, scoring, and explanations then run over that text, and every response is validated and safety-filtered before display.
faq.a8: Yes — sharing creates a temporary, text-only page with your matches that expires automatically. It never contains your photo, which no longer exists by that point.
faq.q9: Why did my round fail or return no match?
faq.a9: Usually the photo was too unclear for confident traits — low light, an extreme angle, heavy filters — or the traits were too generic. The game says so honestly instead of inventing a match; a clearer photo usually fixes it.
faq.a10: The game is designed to be safe and non-judgmental, but it is meant for adults and for teens with a parent's guidance. A parent or guardian should give the consent for any child's photo — and remember: nothing is stored either way.
faq.q11: How accurate is Twinzy, and can it be wrong?
faq.a11: It is a playful estimate, not a measurement, and it can absolutely be wrong — the AI is reading a single photo, not verifying a fact. Each trait carries a confidence level, unclear traits are labelled rather than guessed, and a blurry or badly lit photo will honestly produce a less confident result rather than a falsely precise one.
faq.q12: What photo should I upload for the best result?
faq.a12: A recent, unfiltered photo where your face is clearly lit and mostly facing the camera, with nothing covering your hair, eyes, or jawline. Our guide on choosing a photo covers this with examples of what helps and what does not.
faq.q13: Does lighting or camera angle affect my result?
faq.a13: Yes, more than almost anything else. Strong backlighting, harsh side shadows, and extreme up or down angles all hide the visible detail the AI is trying to read, which shows up as wider uncertainty in your result. Our lighting and camera-angle guides explain exactly why.
faq.q14: What can the AI infer from my photo — and what can't it?
faq.a14: It can describe what is visibly there: hair, glasses, facial hair, face shape, expression, apparent style. It is instructed never to infer ethnicity, religion, health, personality, attractiveness, or income, and never to identify who you are — those limits are enforced in code on every response, not just requested in a prompt.
faq.q15: Is there anything to delete after I play?
faq.a15: No — because nothing was ever kept. Your photo is wiped from server memory immediately after its traits are read, on success, failure, or cancellation alike, so there is no stored image or profile to request deletion of.

privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.metaDescription: How Twinzy handles your photo: one in-memory read into written traits, immediate deletion, no accounts, no biometric data, plus full disclosure of the third-party services and ads that keep the game affordable.
privacy.intro: Twinzy is built to know as little about you as possible.
privacy.photoNotStored: Your photo is never stored. It is processed only to read visible traits, then destroyed.
privacy.traitsOnly: After visible traits are extracted, matching works only with written descriptions like hair color or face shape.
privacy.noFaceRecognition: There is no face recognition, identity matching, or biometric comparison of any kind.
privacy.noTemplates: We never create or keep face templates, embeddings, or any biometric data.
privacy.geminiNote: Our server uses the Google Gemini API to read visible traits and suggest playful matches.
privacy.funOnly: Results are for fun only and can be wrong.
privacy.freeNote: Playing costs only a small, clearly priced fee per analysis, always shown before you pay — and card details go to the payment provider, never to us.
privacy.lifecycleTitle: The life of a photo, in full
privacy.lifecycleBody1: Your photo travels encrypted to our server only after you consent, is held in memory just long enough for visible traits to be written down, and is then wiped — whether the round succeeded, failed, or was cancelled. It is never written to disk, logged, backed up, or used for training.
privacy.lifecycleBody2: Everything after that moment — matching, scoring, translation, sharing — receives only the written traits. There is no copy of the image left to leak, sell, or hand over.
privacy.notCollectedBody1: No accounts, no names, no email addresses, no contact lists, no galleries, no location. We do not build profiles and have no user database.
privacy.notCollectedBody2: Shared result pages are temporary, text-only, and expire on their own; they never include the photo.
privacy.thirdPartiesBody1: Trait extraction uses Google's Gemini API: the photo is sent for that single read under the API's data-usage terms and is not used to train Google's models. Optional payments are processed by PayPal or Paymob — card details go to the payment provider, never to us.
privacy.thirdPartiesBody2: We share no photo, no traits, and no results with advertisers. Ad systems (described below) run only on content pages and are completely separate from the game pipeline.
privacy.advertisingBody1: To keep Twinzy affordable we may show ads from Google AdSense on content pages such as this one — never inside the game and never beside your results. Google and its partners may use cookies to serve and measure ads, including personalized ads where the law allows it.
privacy.advertisingBody2: You can opt out of personalized advertising at adssettings.google.com and read how Google uses ad data at policies.google.com/technologies/ads. The game itself works identically with ads blocked.
privacy.choicesBody1: Play without sharing: results only leave your device if you create a share link. Play without ads: content pages are the only place ads can appear, and blocking them does not affect the game.
privacy.choicesBody2: Because nothing about you is retained, there is no stored data to request or delete — closing the tab is a full erase.

terms.title: Terms
terms.noSeriousUse: Do not use results for identity checks, hiring, dating decisions, or anything serious.
terms.permission: Only upload photos of yourself, or of someone who gave you clear permission.
terms.mayBeWrong: Results are playful guesses based on written traits. They can be wrong.
terms.noHarassment: Do not use results to harass, shame, or judge anyone.

help.title: Help
help.a1: You upload one photo. We read visible traits like hair and face shape as text, destroy the photo, then suggest public figures with a similar overall style/vibe from those written traits.
help.a2: No. Matching works only on written trait descriptions, never on your actual face data.
help.a3: No. It lives in memory just long enough to read the visible traits, then it is destroyed.
help.a4: Only a small fee per analysis — the exact price is always shown clearly before you pay.
help.q5: Why did I get no match?
help.a5: Sometimes the traits are too generic or unclear for a confident playful match. Try a clearer, well-lit photo.
